title: Kakheti
description: The cradle of wine: eight thousand years of winemaking in buried clay qvevri.
L: Kakheti is Georgia's main wine region, in the east, making about 70% of the country's wine. It lies in the Alazani valley, between the Greater Caucasus mountains to the north and the Gombori range. Its capital is Telavi; Sighnaghi is a famous hilltop town. Vineyards cover the valley and the foothills.
Alazani valley, about 70% of Georgia's wine

Kakheti's climate is moderately continental: hot summers, mild to cold winters and enough rain, with the Caucasus blocking cold northern air. The Alazani river and valley give fertile, varied soils. Long, warm autumns ripen grapes fully. Hail can be a risk.
What protects Kakheti from cold northern air?
The Caucasus blocks cold air from the north.

Archaeologists have found grape residue in clay jars in Georgia dating to about 6000 BC, around 8,000 years ago, among the oldest evidence of winemaking in the world. Wine is central to Georgian culture: the supra, a traditional feast, is led by a toastmaster, the tamada, with many long toasts.
Georgia has some of the oldest evidence of winemaking in the world.
Kakheti, in eastern Georgia, makes about 70% of its wine
The Caucasus shelters it; autumns are warm
Georgia has made wine for about 8,000 years

Georgia has over 500 native grape varieties. Rkatsiteli, the most planted white, has high acidity and gives citrus, apple and quince in modern styles, or rich, tannic amber wine in qvevri. Mtsvane Kakhuri, green of Kakheti, is aromatic, with tropical fruit and flowers, often blended with Rkatsiteli. Kisi is another fine white.

Saperavi, meaning dye or colour, is Georgia's main red. It's a teinturier, with red flesh, giving very deep colour, high acidity and firm tannin, with blackberry, black cherry, plum and spice. It ages well. It makes dry reds, like Mukuzani, and semi-sweet reds, like Kindzmarauli.
Match each grape to its character.
Georgia's grapes are native and diverse.
Saperavi's red flesh means even its juice is coloured. Its wines can be almost black.
Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane lead the whites
Saperavi is a red-fleshed, deeply coloured red
Explain how qvevri wine is made

A qvevri is a large, egg-shaped clay vessel, from about 800 to several thousand litres, buried up to its neck in the ground. The inside is coated with beeswax. The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable, around 13 to 15 degrees, during fermentation and ageing. Qvevri are made by hand by a few master potters.

Crushed grapes, often with skins, seeds and sometimes stems, chacha, go into the qvevri. Fermentation starts with native yeasts. The cap is punched down, then the qvevri is sealed with a stone or wooden lid and clay. The wine stays on the skins for months, often until spring. The egg shape helps solids settle at the bottom.
The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable

In 2013, UNESCO added the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri winemaking method to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The method inspired producers worldwide, especially in Friuli, where Josko Gravner began using qvevri in 2001, and in the natural wine movement.
Qvevri winemaking uses clay, not oak.
Qvevri are egg-shaped clay vessels buried in the ground
Grapes ferment with skins for months

In Georgia, white wine made with long skin contact is called amber wine, karvisperi. In Kakheti, the tradition is full skin contact, with all the chacha, for about six months in qvevri. The result is deep amber, tannic and textured. Western Georgia, in Imereti, uses less chacha and shorter contact for lighter wines.

Amber Rkatsiteli tastes of dried apricot, quince, walnuts, honey, black tea and spice, with firm tannin and fresh acidity. It's dry. It's closer to a red wine in structure, so it's served at 12 to 16 degrees and pairs with food. The same grape can also make a fresh, European-style white, with no skin contact.
White wine made with long skin contact

Today Georgia makes both traditional qvevri wines and European-style wines in steel and oak. Both use native grapes. Amber wines are a small but growing share, and exports have surged. They've inspired the orange wine category worldwide, though Georgians prefer the term amber.
Georgian amber wines are usually sweet.
Not true. They're dry, with tannin and acidity.
Amber wine is white wine with long skin contact
Kakhetian amber wine uses full skins for about six months
It's dry, tannic, with dried apricot and walnut
Reading Georgia and eating with it

Georgian wines often name a protected place, like Tsinandali, a white blend of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane; Mukuzani, dry Saperavi; Kindzmarauli, semi-sweet Saperavi; or Napareuli. Labels may say qvevri, amber or the grape. Georgia has about 29 protected appellations. Labels may be in the Georgian alphabet, which is unique.

Georgian food is rich and spiced: khachapuri, cheese bread; khinkali, dumplings; mtsvadi, grilled meat; dishes with walnuts, pomegranate and herbs. Amber wines suit walnut sauces, grilled meat and cheese. Saperavi suits lamb and grilled pork. The supra feast, with its tamada and many toasts, is central to Georgian wine culture.
Who leads the toasts at a Georgian supra?
Kindzmarauli, a semi-sweet Saperavi, is a popular Georgian style; it pairs with spicy food and desserts.
